key_finding: Search effort and answer quality are only weakly aligned; answer accuracy correlates more with cumulative retrieval recall than with number of searches, and top agents issue far fewer redundant queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis with human-annotated document relevance judgments, retrieval model held fixed, comparing six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and validating on BrowseComp with an open-web search API.
why_it_matters: Shows that more agentic search effort does not reliably translate into better answers, undermining the assumption that agentic mechanisms automatically outperform simpler search, and points to recall-based stopping criteria as the metric worth measuring.
limitations: Evaluated on only two benchmark families (BrowseComp-Plus/BrowseComp)
Six agents may not represent the full design space of agentic systems
relevance_reason: Directly decomposes what drives agentic gains (retrieval vs utilization) and shows where search effort fails to help, bearing on both Q2 and Q4.

key_finding: PaSa-7B surpasses the best Google+GPT-4o baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on the real-world RealScholarQuery benchmark.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that invokes search tools, reads papers, and selects references; trained on the synthetic AutoScholarQuery dataset (35k queries) and evaluated on RealScholarQuery against Google/Scholar/ChatGPT baselines.
why_it_matters: Establishes the quantified baseline-vs-agent recall gap for academic paper search and the benchmark construction (AutoScholarQuery/RealScholarQuery) much later work is measured against.
limitations: Training data drawn from top-tier AI conference papers may not generalize to other fields
Comparisons against live Google baselines are hard to reproduce as APIs change
relevance_reason: Closest prior work establishing the quantified agentic-vs-single-query-search gain and the benchmark-construction template underlying it.

key_finding: Crase's bounded 1.5-hop citation-graph expansion with entailment pruning and recency-aware ranking outperforms proprietary deep research agents by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch.
methodology: Single seed search, 1.5-hop citation-neighborhood expansion, entailment-based edge pruning, recency-aware random-walk ranking; evaluated on LitSearch and one further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal as the specific agentic move carrying most of the reported gain, directly answering which mechanism matters and by how much, at lower cost than open-ended agent loops.
limitations: Evaluated on only two benchmarks
arXiv-only corpus may not generalize to other literatures
relevance_reason: Directly attributes a measured recall gain to citation-graph traversal, the exact mechanism the brief asks to isolate.

key_finding: Human- and AI-selected references overlapped less than 6% across eight expert-conceived physics/astrophysics/cosmology projects, and 64% of mid-2025 AI-generated real references had at least one incorrect metadata field, though a 2026 model showed zero fabrications/mismatches in a single test.
methodology: Controlled parallel-task study: human experts and AI systems (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini, ChatGPT Pro 5.5) perform identical literature-review tasks on eight defined research projects; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that agentic/deep-research LLM literature search reliably reproduces expert-quality search, and quantifies a specific failure mode (metadata hallucination) the scan should track as evidence quality degrades.
limitations: Small sample of eight projects in one applied domain
2026-model improvement based on a single project test
relevance_reason: Strongest available contradicting evidence against the premise that agentic literature-search gains are real and reliable.

key_finding: WisPaper achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with its WisModel validator reaching 93.70% validation accuracy against retrieval hallucinations.
methodology: Abstract-only; end-to-end agent system combining keyword search with an agentic 'Deep Search' validation module, evaluated on TaxoBench.
why_it_matters: Shows a deployed system's agentic gain over a strong LLM baseline is modest (~1.3 recall points), a useful data point on how small reported agentic gains can be in practice.
limitations: Gain over baseline is small and could be within noise
TaxoBench's construction is not described in the abstract
relevance_reason: A quantified but modest agentic-vs-baseline gain, useful comparison but replaceable by stronger evidence in this batch.

key_finding: ReBOL, combining LLM query reformulation with Bayesian-optimization-guided batched relevance scoring, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 and 63.6% vs 61.2% NDCG@10 against the best LLM reranker baseline on Robust04.
methodology: Multimodal Bayesian Optimization posterior over document relevance initialized via LLM query reformulations, iteratively updated via batched LLM relevance scoring; evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete retrieval/reranking technique combining query reformulation and relevance optimization that could underlie agentic literature-search systems, though tested on general IR rather than literature search.
limitations: Evaluated on general BEIR datasets, not academic-literature-search benchmarks
No evaluation of citation-graph traversal or crawling mechanisms
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method combining reformulation and Bayesian optimization, relevant to C3 but outside the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: Removing hyperlinks from a wiki-style corpus roughly doubled search cost per grounded fact and made some facts unreachable by literal search yet recoverable through link-derived re-search vocabulary.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm contrast on a deterministic generated corpus (50/500/5000 pages) with/without hyperlinks, evaluated via a Claude agent across 99 episodes; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a weak structural analogy—link-following reduces search cost and reveals otherwise-unreachable content—similar in spirit to citation-graph traversal, but the setting is an organizational wiki, not scientific literature.
limitations: Corpus is a synthetic organizational wiki, not scientific literature
Single agent/model tested
Unclear peer review venue
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence for graph/link structure reducing search cost, offered as an analogy rather than direct evidence in the brief's setting.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding retriever in the loop, matches the best fine-tuned ensemble on BRIGHT (46.7 nDCG@10) and its ensemble variant reaches 49.1 nDCG@10.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchical corpus index over multi-level summaries plus calibrated, path-aggregated LLM traversal; evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that single-query embedding retrieval fails on reasoning-intensive queries even for SOTA embedders, motivating a retrieval architecture that bypasses the vector-search baseline the brief asks us to anchor against.
limitations: Evaluated mainly on general reasoning-IR benchmarks, not literature-search-specific corpora
Needs a moderate token budget before its asymptotic advantage over reranking appears
relevance_reason: Provides both the recall-ceiling failure of standard embedding retrieval and an alternative retrieval/reranking method directly underlying agentic search systems.

key_finding: With a fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 reaches only 3.86% accuracy while GPT-5 reaches 55.9%, and GPT-5 with the Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever reaches 70.1% with fewer search calls.
methodology: Benchmark derived from BrowseComp using a fixed curated corpus with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of retriever versus agent contribution.
why_it_matters: Gives the field's clearest anchored baseline recall ceiling and the benchmark-construction template that later replication-failure studies are measured against.
limitations: Corpus assembled per-query from the benchmark's own supporting documents, later shown to be potentially non-representative
Single snapshot of models tested
relevance_reason: The necessary foundational benchmark for anchoring baseline-vs-agentic gains, central to Q1, Q3, and Q4.

key_finding: NIS-Agent, which isolates context at webpage-triage and answer-validation steps to counter a newly identified 'inertia bias,' achieves competitive performance while cutting token cost by 33% across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark to measure inertia bias, then proposes a context-isolation architecture (NIS-Agent) and trains an 8B model to resist the bias.
why_it_matters: Identifies an additional failure mode (self-authored action bias) degrading deep-research agent judgment, flagging a measurement dimension beyond the three named agentic moves that the scan should watch for.
limitations: Inertia bias is a narrower mechanism than reformulation/graph-traversal/crawling named in the brief
IBIS benchmark is new and not yet independently validated
relevance_reason: Surfaces an additional agentic failure mode and cost-saving fix, informing what to measure though not central to the four named decisions.

key_finding: Structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF chunking, with 68.3% single-pass agentic QA success and 99.0% citation accuracy across 643 evaluated observations.
methodology: ETL+RAG pipeline combining semantic search, keyword filtering, and knowledge-graph traversal with agentic self-correction, applied as a case study to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a hybrid retrieval architecture (semantic + keyword + KG traversal) with measurable citation-accuracy gains, relevant to the retrieval/reranking layer underlying literature-synthesis agents.
limitations: Case study limited to one applied domain (geospatial epidemiology)
No comparison against a single-query database-search baseline
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval/reranking system for literature synthesis with quantified extraction and citation-accuracy gains, useful evidence for the retrieval-method criterion.

key_finding: Provides a taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static/dynamic workflows, single/multi-agent) and a critical evaluation identifying benchmark limitations including restricted external-knowledge access and metric-objective misalignment.
methodology: Abstract-only narrative synthesis and taxonomy across Deep Research agent literature, with a critical review of current benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Orients the scan to the field's existing critique of benchmark construction and agent architecture taxonomy, flagging exactly the benchmark-construction weaknesses (Q3) and evaluation-metric misalignment (Q4) the brief asks about.
limitations: Narrative review with no explicit systematic protocol
Abstract gives no quantified findings
relevance_reason: The field's synthesis and critique of benchmark limitations, providing review-level orientation before weighing individual studies.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus questions onto the independently-built ClimbMix corpus drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% while answer accuracy falls only five points and search calls rise 63%.
methodology: Projection pipeline decomposing questions into atomic reasoning hops, grounding each hop in a new 553M-document corpus (ClimbMix) via automatic verification, independent-agent check, and human review; applied to 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions, yielding 57 fully grounded questions.
why_it_matters: Shows a widely-used benchmark's reported recall inflates because its corpus was assembled per-query, and that agentic evidence-recall gains shrink dramatically once relocated to a corpus built without benchmark awareness — the replication-failure evidence the brief is looking for.
limitations: Pipeline yields only 57 grounded questions out of 830, a small evaluated subset
Only a single projection target (ClimbMix) tested so far
relevance_reason: The clearest demonstration that a benchmark's construction inflates agentic gains and that those gains fail to hold under an independently-built corpus.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Multi-turn agent trained via supervised workflow imitation and preference optimization over workflow corruptions; DAG of search operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction), evaluated against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset agent baseline. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly targets question 2 by making the workflow itself (not the system as a whole) the unit of measurement, decomposing citation expansion/reranking into an editable DAG rather than free-form reasoning.
limitations: Baseline is a toolset agent, not a single-query database search ceiling
No discussion of benchmark construction or contamination controls
9B model scale limits generalization claims
relevance_reason: A concrete, quantified agentic literature-search system decomposing search into an editable operator workflow, squarely on the brief's system-design question.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided query reformulation for graph retrieval exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Separates residual query reformulation from graph evidence aggregation, normalizing and combining original/residual retrieval signals; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Isolates a query-reformulation-plus-graph-propagation mechanism with a measured gain, the same C2/C3 pattern the brief wants for literature-search agents, but demonstrated on general multi-hop QA rather than scientific literature retrieval.
limitations: Evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature search
No comparison to literature-search-specific baselines
Abstract gives no ablation isolating reformulation from propagation
relevance_reason: Method precedent for query-reformulation-driven graph retrieval gain attribution, but off the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: Across 24 runnable AI-scientist systems audited, 83% release code but only 38% release execution traces/seeds and 38% report any novelty-verification method, and no LLM-era closed-loop system demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Systematic screening of 125 candidate works, full-text coding of 26 entries across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation method, artifacts, human-in-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure). Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Frames literature search as one stage within a broader verification-gap problem in autonomous research agents, useful context for how much to trust self-reported gains, but not itself a mechanism- or benchmark-specific answer to the four questions.
limitations: Literature search is only one of many lifecycle stages covered, not the focus
Does not decompose agentic search mechanisms or benchmark construction specifics
Abstract-only
relevance_reason: A broad audit of reproducibility/verification practice across AI-scientist systems, relevant context but not decision-changing for the specific search-mechanism questions.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves 16.5x higher F1 than Google Scholar and 37.8% higher F1 than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost across 38 disciplines in PaSaMaster-Bench, while reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving retrieval agent that refines search intent from ranked evidence, ranks only verified papers, and separates planning (frontier LLM) from retrieval/scoring (lightweight models); evaluated on a custom 38-discipline benchmark. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Puts an explicit, quantified number on the single-query-search ceiling (Google Scholar) versus an agentic system, directly anchoring question 1 and attributing gain to a specific self-evolving retrieval mechanism for question 2.
limitations: Benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) is self-constructed with limited independent scrutiny
No detail in the abstract on relevance-labeling methodology or contamination control
Comparison against GPT-5.2 conflates model capability with agentic design
relevance_reason: The clearest literature-search-specific quantification of agentic gain over a plain single-query search baseline, exactly what question 1 asks for.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature search tasks and identifies 2.34\u00b11.99 contradictions per biology paper, 70% validated by human experts, using the newly introduced LitQA2 benchmark.
methodology: Rigorous human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature search tasks (retrieval, summarization, contradiction detection); introduces LitQA2, a hard benchmark that guided PaperQA2's design. Abstract-only beyond stated figures.
why_it_matters: The landmark result the field argues with: the strongest published claim that agentic search now beats domain experts, so any assessment of whether agentic gains are real has to be read against this paper's benchmark and claims specifically.
limitations: No explicit single-query database search baseline recall reported for comparison
Benchmark (LitQA2) co-designed with the system it evaluates, raising circularity concerns
Domain restricted largely to biology
relevance_reason: Foundational/closest prior work for the whole scan: the paper whose 'superhuman' claim this brief's question 4 is designed to test.

key_finding: Grep-based retrieval generally yields higher accuracy than vector (embedding) retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample across Chronos and provider CLI harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), though scores still depend strongly on harness and tool-calling style.
methodology: Two-experiment empirical comparison: grep vs vector retrieval across multiple agent harnesses with inline vs file-based tool outputs, plus a distractor-injection experiment mixing in unrelated conversation history. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the assumption that embedding/vector search is the stronger baseline retrieval method underlying agentic search, exactly the kind of check question 1 needs before crediting any 'agentic' gain to retrieval sophistication rather than harness plumbing.
limitations: Evaluated on conversational memory (LongMemEval), not scientific literature corpora
Findings may be harness-specific rather than retrieval-method-general
No literature-search-specific benchmark used
relevance_reason: A rigorous within-harness comparison showing a simpler exact-match baseline beating vector retrieval, a direct method transfer bearing on whether reported agentic gains are retrieval-sophistication or harness-design artifacts.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically maps the conditions (fact retrieval vs. complex reasoning vs. summarization vs. creative generation) under which graph structure actually helps.
methodology: Comprehensive benchmark with tasks of increasing difficulty, evaluating the full GraphRAG pipeline from graph construction and retrieval through generation, compared against vanilla RAG. Abstract-only for detailed numbers.
why_it_matters: Directly answers question 4 for the graph-traversal mechanism specifically: the citation/graph-traversal 'agentic move' does not reliably beat plain retrieval, and the paper gives task-level conditions for when it does \u2014 exactly the evidence the brief says it should reach hardest for.
limitations: General-purpose RAG benchmark, not scientific-literature-search specific
Abstract does not give the numeric size of the underperformance
Findings tied to the specific GraphRAG implementations tested
relevance_reason: The single strongest piece of evidence in this batch that a core agentic mechanism (graph traversal) fails to reliably beat single-query-style baseline RAG, directly serving question 4.

key_finding: DynaKRAG ranks first in EM and F1 across all nine dataset-backbone pairs (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue x three LLM backbones) versus matched baselines, with 10.1-34.3% token efficiency gains and 15.1-43.4% fewer retrieval calls.
methodology: Unified evidence-action policy coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, evidence assessment, and sufficiency checking via a learned continuation gate and advantage scorer. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: A methods precedent for decomposing 'iterative retrieval + reformulation + sufficiency checking' into a learned, measurable policy \u2014 the mechanism-attribution pattern question 2 wants \u2014 but demonstrated on general multi-hop QA rather than literature search.
limitations: Evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks, not literature search
No single-query database search baseline reported directly
Efficiency gains reported relative to a matched-backbone baseline, not a plain search ceiling
relevance_reason: Closely related mechanism-decomposition method for iterative retrieval/reformulation, but the setting is general QA rather than the brief's literature-search domain.

key_finding: Search-time contamination (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, explicit answer leakage) is widespread in deep research agent evaluation and can inflate measured performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks.
methodology: Defines three contamination types with increasing severity and develops detection algorithms to identify and quantify them across modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly answers question 4: a concrete, quantified mechanism (search-time leakage) by which reported agentic gains on public benchmarks are inflated rather than real \u2014 exactly the failure-to-hold-up evidence the brief says it must reach hardest for.
limitations: 4% inflation figure reported across six general benchmarks, not literature-search-specific ones
Detection algorithms' false-positive/negative rates not given in the abstract
Does not decompose which specific agentic mechanism benefits most from contamination
relevance_reason: The clearest available evidence that reported agentic-search gains partly reflect benchmark contamination rather than genuine capability, the core of question 4.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's 89 multi-step web research tasks show offline 'RetroSearch' agents (using a frozen scraped-web corpus) perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling reliable evaluation over time as the web changes.
methodology: 89 task instances across 8 categories with human-worked answers; frozen web-page corpus environment contrasted with live search; automated evaluation of agent traces for hallucination, tool use, and forgetting; benchmarking of major LLMs and branded 'Deep Research' products. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete benchmark-construction precedent for controlling one of the biggest confounds in evaluating search agents (a continually-changing live web / contamination), directly informing question 3 on how evaluation sets should be built.
limitations: Web research tasks generally, not specifically scientific literature search
89 task instances is a modest sample for fine-grained mechanism attribution
Comparability of RetroSearch vs live agents shown only in aggregate, not per-mechanism
relevance_reason: A benchmark-construction precedent (frozen corpus for reproducible, contamination-resistant evaluation) directly bearing on how the brief's benchmarks should be built.

key_finding: The leading MTEB embedding retriever (SFR-Embedding-Mistral, 59.0 nDCG@10 on standard benchmarks) scores only 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries, though explicit query reasoning recovers up to 12.2 points.
methodology: 1,384 real-world, reasoning-intensive queries curated across economics, psychology, mathematics, and coding domains; extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art retrieval models. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Sets the single clearest, most quantified ceiling for single-query embedding-search recall under reasoning-intensive queries \u2014 the exact anchor question 1 needs before any agentic literature-search gain can be judged credible or inflated.
limitations: Domains are economics/psychology/math/coding, not scientific-literature retrieval directly
Predates most 2025-2026 agentic literature-search systems
Gain from explicit reasoning (12.2 points) still leaves a large residual gap unexplained
relevance_reason: Foundational baseline-ceiling result establishing how badly plain embedding search fails on reasoning-heavy queries, the anchor question 1 requires.

key_finding: Agents-K1 converts 2.46 million scientific papers into agent-native knowledge graphs (Scholar-KG) using a multimodal parser, a 4B GRPO-trained extraction backbone, and a tri-source retrieval CLI unifying web search, graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal, achieving superior performance on scientific IE, KG construction, and multi-hop reasoning.
methodology: Large-scale pipeline processing 2.46M papers across six subjects, releasing a one-million-paper subset; multimodal five-module parsing schema plus reinforcement-learned extraction model. Abstract-only for exact benchmark numbers.
why_it_matters: A concrete, large-scale demonstration of citation-graph traversal plus cross-document reasoning as the agentic mechanism, and a corpus/benchmark construction precedent at a scale most other papers in this scan lack \u2014 directly informs question 2 (graph traversal mechanism) and question 3 (corpus coverage).
limitations: Abstract omits quantitative gains over single-query or non-graph baselines
No discussion of contamination or relevance-labeling methodology for the derived benchmark
Released subset (1M of 2.46M papers) may not represent full corpus difficulty
relevance_reason: A large-scale, citation-graph-centric literature-knowledge system directly instantiating the graph-traversal mechanism and corpus-construction questions the brief asks about.

key_finding: An agent that dynamically selects between GraphRAG and VectorRAG, with DPO-tuned generation, gains 0.63 in Vector-Store Context Recall and 0.56 in overall Context Precision over baseline on synthetic benchmark queries.
methodology: Neo4j citation knowledge graph plus FAISS vector store over PubMed/arXiv/Google Scholar data; Llama-3.3-70B agent chooses GraphRAG vs VectorRAG per query; evaluated with bootstrapped metrics on synthetic benchmark queries. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: An open-source instantiation of dynamic hybrid retrieval selection for literature review, but evaluated only on synthetic rather than real relevance-labeled queries, so it is illustrative rather than decision-changing evidence for the benchmark-construction question.
limitations: Evaluated on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real queries, not real relevance-labeled literature-search tasks
No comparison against a single-query search ceiling
Small citation count / early-stage system
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic hybrid agentic RAG system for literature review, useful as a design example but replaceable by stronger evidence already in the set.

key_finding: A keyword-based sparse retrieval and distillation system achieves results close to state of the art on biology literature-review benchmarks without needing dense retrieval, while also increasing coverage of relevant documents.
methodology: LLM-based agentic search-and-distillation system evaluated against existing biology literature benchmarks; abstract-only for quantitative specifics.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the added infrastructure of dense/complex retrieval is necessary, bearing on the baseline recall-ceiling question the brief treats as foundational.
limitations: biology domain only
abstract gives no quantitative numbers
single system, no ablation isolating which agentic move drove coverage gains
relevance_reason: Challenges the premise that dense retrieval or added complexity is required to match strong baselines, directly informing the recall-ceiling question.

key_finding: Roughly 3% of questions on HLE, SimpleQA, and GPQA are answerable by search agents copying leaked ground-truth from HuggingFace, and blocking HuggingFace drops accuracy on the contaminated subset by about 15%.
methodology: Empirical audit of search-based agent logs across three benchmarks, with ablation experiments (blocking HuggingFace) and publicly released logs.
why_it_matters: Shows that a measurable slice of reported agentic-search performance is an artifact of benchmark leakage rather than genuine capability, directly demanding contamination controls for any literature-search benchmark's numbers.
limitations: evaluated on general QA benchmarks, not literature-search-specific ones
contamination source identified only partially (HuggingFace)
relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence that reported agentic-search gains can fail to replicate once contamination is controlled for \u2014 exactly the hardest evidence the brief asks the scan to find.

key_finding: CG-RAG's graph-integrated hybrid sparse-dense retrieval (LeSeGR) over citation graphs significantly outperforms RAG methods paired with state-of-the-art retrieval approaches on research question-answering benchmarks.
methodology: Contextual citation-graph representation combined with hybrid lexical-semantic graph retrieval and graph-aware generation, tested across multiple research-QA benchmarks; abstract-only for numbers.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal plus hybrid retrieval as the specific mechanism producing gains, which is the C2 attribution (mechanism vs. undifferentiated system) the brief asks for.
limitations: no explicit numeric gains in the abstract
benchmark construction not described
generalizability across literature domains untested
relevance_reason: Directly evaluates citation-graph traversal as a distinct agentic mechanism underlying retrieval gains, central to the brief's second question.

key_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs achieve only 0.40 accuracy on FRAMES with no retrieval, rising to 0.66 (>50% relative improvement) with a proposed multi-step retrieval pipeline on challenging multi-hop questions.
methodology: New multi-domain unified RAG evaluation dataset (FRAMES) testing factuality, retrieval, and reasoning jointly, with baseline vs. multi-step retrieval pipeline comparisons.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete, widely-cited no-retrieval baseline number against which any claimed agentic-search improvement in this space should be measured.
limitations: general multi-hop QA rather than a scientific-literature corpus
does not decompose which specific agentic move drove the multi-step gain
relevance_reason: Gives the clearest quantified baseline-vs-pipeline comparison anchoring the brief's recall-ceiling and benchmark-construction questions.

key_finding: Across 130 long-horizon, real-time web tasks, the best agentic search system (OpenAI Deep Research) reaches only 50-70% of human performance despite using half the time, scored via a new Agent-as-Judge rubric framework.
methodology: New benchmark (Mind2Web 2) built with over 1000 hours of human labor and a tree-structured rubric "Agent-as-Judge" evaluation method; ten frontier agentic search systems and humans compared.
why_it_matters: Supplies the closest available precedent for constructing and scoring open-ended, long-horizon agentic-search benchmarks \u2014 directly transferable to the rubric-based scoring literature-search benchmarks will need.
limitations: general web search rather than scientific literature specifically
no comparison against a single-query baseline search
relevance_reason: Its Agent-as-Judge rubric-based scoring methodology is the closest available benchmark-construction template for evaluating open-ended literature-search agents.

key_finding: An LLM-guided knowledge-graph traversal method using memory replay of traversal experience in edge embeddings improves both effectiveness and cost efficiency of KG-RAG over existing baselines.
methodology: Train-free graph traversal (node exploration, exploitation, memory replay) tested across multiple benchmark datasets and LLM backbones; abstract-only for numbers.
why_it_matters: A specific graph-traversal mechanism for cost-efficient retrieval that could inform citation-graph traversal design, but tested only on generic knowledge graphs rather than literature-search corpora.
limitations: general KG-RAG setting, not scientific literature search
no comparison against a single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: Graph traversal technique analogous to citation-graph traversal, but its evaluation setting is outside the brief's literature-search focus.

key_finding: A three-agent (Query/Retrieval/Learning) hybrid BM25+FAISS literature-search system reports an 8.5% precision improvement, 7.3% recall improvement, and ~210ms latency reduction versus PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture combining sparse (BM25) and dense (FAISS/Sentence-Transformers) retrieval, evaluated experimentally against existing literature-search tools.
why_it_matters: Directly attributes measured gains to a specific agentic component (query expansion/refinement) and hybrid retrieval design, exactly the mechanism-attribution the brief's second question asks for.
limitations: no venue listed and very low citation count, suggesting limited vetting
comparison baselines (PaperQA, Semantic Scholar) are not strictly single-query database search
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic system in the brief's setting that attributes quantified precision/recall gains to a specific agentic mechanism (query reformulation).

key_finding: Existing agentic-RAG benchmarks rely on static, fixed corpora and pre-defined gold document sets unsuited to dynamic real-world web information seeking; InfoDeepSeek introduces a systematic query-construction methodology (determinacy, difficulty, diversity) and fine-grained metrics to address this.
methodology: New benchmark with an explicit query-construction methodology and evaluation framework, tested across multiple LLMs, search engines, and question types; abstract-only for numeric results.
why_it_matters: Names the exact benchmark-construction failure modes (fixed corpus, static gold sets) that make differently-built agentic-search benchmarks non-comparable, directly informing the brief's benchmark-construction question.
limitations: general web information seeking rather than literature-specific corpora
no quantitative benchmark numbers given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides an explicit critique and remedy for benchmark-construction weaknesses directly transferable to how literature-search benchmarks should be built and judged.

key_finding: An LLM agentic pipeline that extracts contribution claims, retrieves prior work via semantic search, and produces evidence-grounded novelty reports was deployed on over 500 ICLR 2026 submissions, reportedly surfacing closely related papers authors may have overlooked.
methodology: Four-phase agentic pipeline (query extraction, semantic-search retrieval, taxonomy construction, synthesis) deployed at scale; evaluation described only as "preliminary analysis," abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows an applied literature-retrieval agent in real deployment but does not measure baseline recall, isolate a specific mechanism's gain, or describe benchmark construction, limiting its evidentiary weight.
limitations: application is novelty assessment rather than literature search per se
no quantitative retrieval evaluation
preliminary/informal analysis only
relevance_reason: An applied agentic literature-retrieval pipeline useful as a design example, but not evidentiary on the brief's core recall, mechanism, benchmark, or replication questions.

key_finding: A systematic four-stage taxonomy (planning, question developing, web exploration, report generation) organizes deep-research agent designs, along with the optimization techniques and benchmarks used to evaluate them.
methodology: Narrative/systematic survey categorizing methods and benchmarks for autonomous deep-research agents; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Maps which specific agentic moves the field currently credits with performance gains and which benchmarks are used to measure them, giving the scan an organizing structure against which its other findings can be checked.
limitations: survey rather than primary evidence
does not quantify each stage's individual contribution
framed around general 'deep research' rather than literature-search specifically
relevance_reason: The synthesis paper mapping agentic-search mechanisms and benchmarks onto a single taxonomy, providing orientation across the brief's three in-scope topics.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B, trained on synthetic hard-query/hard-negative data, achieves 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on the BRIGHT reasoning-retrieval benchmark and improves RAG performance on MMLU (+6.4%) and GPQA (+22.6%) over closed-book baselines.
methodology: Synthetic training-data generation pipeline for reasoning-intensive dense retrieval; open-sourced 8B retriever evaluated on BRIGHT and downstream RAG tasks.
why_it_matters: A concrete dense-retriever training method that could underlie the retrieval layer of future literature-search agents, but it is tested on general reasoning benchmarks, not literature-search corpora.
limitations: evaluated on BRIGHT/MMLU/GPQA, not scientific-literature-search benchmarks
no test on literature-search recall specifically
relevance_reason: A state-of-the-art retriever-training technique for reasoning-intensive queries, a candidate component for literature-search agents, but evaluated outside the brief's setting.

key_finding: OpenScholar-8B, retrieving from 45 million open-access papers, outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on the new ScholarQABench benchmark (2,967 queries), while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78-90% of the time versus OpenScholar's expert-level citation accuracy.
methodology: Retrieval-augmented LM with a dedicated 45M-paper datastore, retriever, and self-feedback inference loop, evaluated on a newly built multi-domain benchmark (ScholarQABench) plus human preference studies.
why_it_matters: The closest existing system to what the brief is scoping \u2014 a full literature-search-and-synthesis agent with its own purpose-built benchmark and quantified baseline comparisons \u2014 making it the primary comparison point for design and evaluation decisions.
limitations: domain coverage limited to CS/physics/neuroscience/biomedicine
self-feedback loop's specific contribution not isolated from the rest of the system
relevance_reason: Closest prior work to the system the brief is scoping, with its own purpose-built benchmark and quantified gains over strong baselines.

key_finding: On 597 realistic literature-search queries, BM25 trails state-of-the-art dense retrievers by 24.8 points of absolute recall@5, LLM-based reranking further improves the best dense retriever by 4.4%, and commercial search engines/Google lag the best dense retriever by 32 points.
methodology: New retrieval benchmark (LitSearch) built from GPT-4-generated questions over cited paragraphs plus author-written questions about their own recent papers, all expert-verified; extensive benchmarking of retrievers, rerankers, and commercial search engines.
why_it_matters: Gives the single clearest, quantified statement of the baseline recall ceiling (BM25 vs. dense vs. commercial search) that every later agentic-search claim in this space should be measured against.
limitations: restricted to ML/NLP papers
queries partly LLM-generated rather than naturally occurring
does not test full multi-step agentic search pipelines
relevance_reason: The foundational quantified baseline and benchmark-construction template anchoring the brief's recall-ceiling and benchmark-construction questions.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, a 100-task PhD-level benchmark across 22 fields with two novel evaluation methodologies (reference-based report quality assessment and citation-based retrieval accuracy) shown to align strongly with human judgment.
methodology: Benchmark construction: 100 tasks crafted by domain experts, plus two evaluation frameworks — a reference-based adaptive-criteria scorer for report quality and an effective-citation-count/citation-accuracy framework for retrieval assessment. Abstract-only beyond this.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the benchmark-construction question the brief prioritizes third: it specifies query/task source (expert-crafted PhD-level tasks), a concrete relevance/quality labeling scheme, and a citation-accuracy metric for retrieval — the kind of construction detail needed to judge whether other systems' reported gains are comparable across benchmarks.
limitations: abstract gives no numeric results or agent comparisons, so it cannot speak to C1 recall ceilings or C5 replication failures
focused on report-quality and citation-accuracy evaluation rather than isolating which agentic mechanism (reformulation, graph traversal, crawling) drives gains
tasks are PhD-level general research tasks, not verified against a single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: One of the few in-scope papers giving concrete benchmark-construction detail (task sourcing, labeling, citation-based retrieval metric) that the brief's C4 criterion asks for, making it a benchmark precedent later agentic-search evaluations would be measured against.
